entries.title: House Votes a Third Time to End the Iran War as Conflict Drags On
entries.summary: A few more Republicans joined the mostly Democratic effort to end the conflict.
entries.content:
By Lisa Mascaro

For a third time, the U.S. House has voted to end the war in Iran, approving a war powers resolution that would halt President Donald Trump's ability to continue military action without congressional approval.

The roll call late Tuesday, 220-204, was similar to earlier efforts this summer, with a few more Republicans joining most Democrats voting to bring an end to the conflict. None of the resolutions have made it to the president's desk, where Trump would almost certainly veto the measure.

“Remember when Donald Trump said that this war would last just a few weeks?” said Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., who served as a Marine during the Iraq war and pushed the resolution forward.

He said it's time for Congress to “actually ask tough questions, as the Constitution directs us to do, rather than be subservient to another warmongering administration.”

Republican Rep. Brian Mast of Florida, the chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, questioned which military resources Democrats would want to remove from the region where he said Iran remains a threat.

Mast said Trump is against “forever wars, and that is what he is ending” — the decades of hostilities from Iran.

“They are a continuous ongoing threat to the United States," Mast said. “Enough is enough.”

Last war powers vote before the midterms

The action is likely the last House vote on the Iran war ahead of the midterm elections, where the conflict overseas is playing a substantial role in the political campaigns. The war that Trump launched Feb. 28 has dragged, with on-again, off-again deadly missile strikes being exchanged and causing havoc in the region for nearly seven months.

Lawmakers are heading home at the end of the week to campaign nearly full-time, with less than 50 days to go before the elections that will determine control of Congress as Democrats try to wrest power from Republicans.

Voters are confronting high prices, particularly for gas at the pumps, as the conflict disrupts the flow of oil resources through the vital Strait of Hormuz.

The Congressional Budget Office said Tuesday that the war has cost more than $38 billion, as of Aug. 1, and is projected to be costing between $2 billion and $3 billion monthly, depending on the intensity of the fighting. The budget office projected inflation will be 0.5 percentage points higher than expected heading into 2027 due to the war.

Trump himself had promised not to involve the U.S. in foreign wars when he won a second term in the White House, and his actions against Iran are weighing on the Republican Party that controls the House and Senate. Most Americans say the war in Iran has not been worth fighting, according to an AP-NORC poll in July.

War powers being put to the test

Congress has tried repeatedly to alter the trajectory of the war against Iran, but efforts to limit the Trump administration's military action remain a longshot so long as the president is able to fend off or veto the measures.

The House first approved a war powers resolution in June, and followed up with another one in July, all seeking to halt U.S. action in Iran. The Senate on its 10th try also approved a war powers resolution to end the conflict, but GOP senators quickly reversed course the next day after Trump berated them during a closed-door lunch.

While the Constitution gives Congress the authority to declare war, it also enables the president authority as the commander in chief to engage in some military actions. The war powers act, created in the aftermath of the Vietnam conflict, sought to put a more specific time limit on the president's power, requiring congressional approval for sustained military actions after 60 or 90 days.

House Speaker Mike Johnson acknowledged at a press conference Tuesday the need to bring gas prices down.

But the Republican speaker said he believes the Iran conflict is entering a “new phase” as allies step up to help stabilize the region. When that happens, he said, “you’re going to see, as the president said, anytime gas prices will go down again, the cost of groceries will as well.”

Johnson said Trump expects the shift after the election, and the speaker added, “I'd love it to happen today.”

entries.title: Beatty Says Trump ‘Threw a Tantrum’ Over Kennedy Center Ruling
entries.summary: The Ohio Democrat says the president called her incompetent, so she returned the name-calling.
entries.content:
Rep. Joyce Beatty said President Donald Trump shouted insults at her during a Kennedy Center board meeting Tuesday after a court blocked his latest effort to put his name on the building.

The Ohio Democrat, an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center board, is suing Trump and the board he stocked with allies over their efforts to add his name to the storied performing arts center. Beatty says the meeting became a “tit for tat” between her and Trump, after she said he phoned into a Tuesday board meeting to berate her.

“It should be unthinkable for someone to hear a president using the language that he used. He threw a tantrum. It was like an immature child,” she told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins on Tuesday.

“I was not going to let him tell me that he thought I was incompetent,” Beatty added. “So I responded by telling him I knew he was incompetent.”

The phone call came just moments after the Kennedy Center board voted to temporarily close its main building for a $250 million renovation. The project's future is now uncertain, though, after Trump announced that construction will not proceed unless his name is added to the building.

At the virtual meeting, Beatty said Trump threatened to hold her personally responsible if someone died because of the building’s condition.

Beatty accused Trump of “trying to hold the board hostage” and said she has never opposed repairs to make the building safe.

“He thought trying to bully me was going to stop me from standing up for what's right,” she said. “He picked the wrong person.”

entries.title: Nationals 6, Philllies 3: Game Recap
entries.summary: Pinch-hitter Daylen Lile hit a tiebreaking three-run homer in the seventh inning.
entries.content:
By Patrick Stevens

Pinch-hitter Daylen Lile hit a tiebreaking three-run homer in the seventh inning, and the Washington Nationals defeated the Philadelphia Phillies 6-3 on Tuesday night.

Andrés Chaparro also homered for Washington, which won its fourth in a row for the first time since June 13-16.

Kyle Schwarber hit his majors-leading 45th homer for Philadelphia, which has dropped four of five but continues to hold an NL wild-card spot.

With the game tied at 3-all, Phillies starter Cristopher Sánchez (17-6) surrendered consecutive singles to open the seventh before Nasim Nuñez bunted both runners over. Philadelphia interim manager Don Mattingly summoned Jonathan Bowlan, and Lile hammered his first pitch to center for his first career pinch homer.

Sánchez allowed five runs and struck out five. He is 1-2 with a 6.87 ERA in three September starts, and his season ERA has risen from 2.52 to 2.93 since the start of the month.

Richard Lovelady (3-4) got the last out of the seventh and two in the eighth for Washington. Erik Tolman pitched a 1-2-3 ninth for his third save.

Schwarber lined Washington starter Jackson Kent’s slider into the Nationals’ bullpen in right to lead off the fifth inning. It is Schwarber’s fourth 45-homer season in five years with the Phillies, tying him with Ryan Howard (2006-09) for the most in franchise history.

Chaparro responded with a solo homer in the fifth off Sánchez.

The Phillies scored in the first inning on Alec Bohm’s RBI single. Yohandy Morales doubled in Washington’s first run in the first, then scored two batters later on Jorbit Vivas’ single.

Luis Arraez’s opposite-field double to left brought in Trea Turner to tie it in the third.

Kent allowed three runs and struck out four in five innings.

Phillies RHP Zack Wheeler (12-5, 3.14 ERA) faces Nationals RHP Cade Cavalli (12-5, 3.12) as the two-game series concludes Wednesday.

entries.title: Chuck Edwards Claims Ethics Committee Coerced Him During Investigation
entries.summary: The House censured the North Carolina Republican over “inappropriate conduct” with staffers.
entries.content:
Rep. Chuck Edwards is accusing the leaders of the House Ethics Committee of bypassing their own rules and using a “coerced” waiver to deny him a fair hearing before the House overwhelmingly censured him over his conduct toward two young female staffers.

In a complaint letter to the Office of Congressional Conduct, the North Carolina Republican contends top House Ethics lawmakers “shamelessly abandoned” their responsibility to provide a fair investigation after allegations surfaced that his conduct toward the staffers created a hostile work environment.

The letter, dated Sept. 2, was sent a day after the House voted 413-2 to censure Edwards. His office published it alongside a press release Tuesday night.

“There was nothing ethical about this process,” Edwards said. “They decided the outcome, adopted their report before receiving my response, denied me the procedures designed to test their accusations, and then publicly attacked my character based on findings that were never subjected to an adjudicatory hearing.”

The Ethics Committee interviewed 16 witnesses as part of a review of nearly 1,500 pages of documented evidence during a four-month investigation. The committee found Edwards sent handwritten notes and poetry to the aides and gave them lavish gifts, intimate dinners and expensive trips.

While the panel found no evidence that Edwards made explicit sexual propositions to his staffers, it ruled his actions violated House sexual harassment policies and created a hostile work environment.

The letter specifically names the Ethics Committee chair, Rep. Michael Guest (R-Mississippi), and its ranking member, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier (D-California), as the subjects of the Edwards allegation.

Over the course of the investigation, Edwards contends the committee omitted directly contrary evidence of his misconduct and did not provide the draft report to Edwards’ counsel until July 31. At that point, the letter states, the investigation had already concluded with a recommendation for censure.

“They could not prove that I violated the law or identify sexual conduct,” Edwards said in his release Tuesday. “So they relied on insinuation, selective evidence, and subjective assumptions — while denying me the very process their rules establish for separating facts from accusations.”

Edwards is calling for an independent investigation and a public apology for the “grave and lasting damage inflicted upon Edwards’ character, dignity, reputation, family, and public service.”

Guest and DeSaulnier had said Edwards agreed to waive certain procedural steps in the investigation. Spokespeople for Guest and DeSaulnier did not immediately respond to The Washington Sun’s request for comment.

entries.title: Trayon White Trial Hinges on One Question: Bribery or Setup?
entries.summary: White is the first sitting D.C. elected official to go to trial for an alleged crime since his self-professed political mentor, Marion Barry.
entries.content:
As the first day of Trayon White’s trial on Tuesday wound to a close, the contours of each side’s strategy had come into focus: Prosecutors intend to argue that the D.C. council member’s conduct two summers ago constituted brazen bribery, while defense attorneys says their client was set up by a corrupt family member coordinating with the FBI in an attempt to escape prison time for his own crimes.

The proceedings unfolded as White — the bespectacled representative of the city’s poorest ward — watched attentively, his expression largely muted, taking notes and occasionally whispering with his attorneys. The three-term lawmaker ended the day on a positive note, posting a selfie on Instagram with the caption: “Still standing tall. Love y’all.”

White, who maintains his innocence, was arrested and indicted in 2024. The council member stands accused of accepting $35,000 in bribes in exchange for agreeing to use his office to influence contracts, after videos showed White exchanging money with an associate and discussing plans to further his business with the D.C. government.

While other city lawmakers have pleaded guilty to crimes in recent decades, White is the first sitting D.C. elected official to go to trial for an alleged crime since his self-professed political mentor, Marion Barry, the larger-than-life former mayor who in 1990 was caught smoking crack cocaine by an FBI sting operation.

The legal process that unfolds in the coming weeks will determine not only White’s personal and political future, but also the future representation of his approximately 87,000 constituents in Ward 8, where he has both staunch critics and staunch defenders. If convicted, White faces potential prison time and will become immediately ineligible for public office in the District. If acquitted, he may remain in office — unless his colleagues on the council vote to expel him.

Prosecutor John Crabb Jr., in the government’s opening statement, harped on one sentence he said White uttered to his associate Allieu Kamara during a surreptitiously recorded meeting in the summer of 2024: “Once you get me, if you lock eyes and get your understanding — I get to work.”

“We will prove to you that by locking eyes and getting to work, Mr. White means selling his office as a D.C. Council member,” Crabb told the jury. The attorney then offered a preview of what the government would come to argue were White’s motives for accepting the cash: campaign debts, $100,000 he needed for a real estate venture he hoped to get in on in North Carolina, and the lawmaker’s alleged statement that “it’s really expensive to see girls and have fun.”

White’s attorney, Gary Kohlman, called Kamara, the government informant seen on video handing White envelopes of money, a “snitch” in his opening statement. Kamara began cooperating with the FBI after the agency investigated him for pandemic loan fraud and bribery of another D.C. government official — charges to which he has since pleaded guilty — and is “corrupt to the bone,” Kohlman said.

He also described an aspect of the two men’s relationship that the government had not mentioned: Kamara was once married to White’s half-sister, he said.

“It’s almost biblical,” said Kohlman, using “one family member to try to set up another.”

Kamara told The Washington Post on Tuesday that it was “not true” that the two men were brothers-in-law. Lloyd Liu, an attorney for Kamara, declined to comment to The Washington Sun regarding the defense’s statements about their family connection.

Kohlman said Kamara had thrown out the names of other D.C. officials who allegedly took bribes — including Democratic Mayor Muriel E. Bowser — to paint a picture of him giving agents any name he could think of to get out of jail. A spokesperson for Bowser declined to comment on the defense’s statements about the mayor.

The jury will have final word in the trial — a case that has at times divided Washingtonians along lines of race and class, as some of White’s defenders have argued that he is the victim of a justice system stacked against Black people and Black political leaders. Of the 14 jurors — a group which includes two alternates — about five appeared to be Black, though the identities of jurors are kept private.

On Tuesday, the government presented video recordings of White and Kamara meeting in his car throughout the course of the summer of 2024. Kamara had agreed to have the meetings surreptitiously recorded by the FBI, and the federal agents gave him cash to hand to White.

The meetings, the lead FBI agent on the case testified, were an attempt to recreate an alleged prior corrupt relationship between the men, in which Kamara told the agency he had bribed White in 2019 in exchange for promising to help with a city contract dispute. The FBI began investigating White in 2023, the agent said, while Kamara emerged as a potential confidential source later in early 2024.

The videoed conversations in that car were at times intimate. White shared how the stresses of his job and his repeated exposure to death had driven him to therapy. In one video, he vented about the city’s treatment of people in his ward displaced by a fire, complaining that the mayor didn’t care about poor people or Black people.

In another, he talked about romantic problems and wondered aloud whether his relationship was the right fit. White later shared that he was “financially bankrupt,” in part because he was giving money to support people who were asking him for it. The two men frequently ended the conversations by saying they loved each other.

The two men also talked business, the videos show. Kamara told the council member he needed help ensuring that his lucrative city contracts would continue. White agreed to ask various city officials about Kamara’s grants — including D.C. Deputy Mayor for Public Safety Lindsey Appiah and Office of Neighborhood Safety and Engagement Director Kwelli Sneed, both of whom are expected to testify. White also suggested future potential plans for the two in the mental health space — an area of city work that he called a “cash cow.”

White’s legal team isn’t planning to dispute that he accepted the cash from Kamara, but rather question whether he actively solicited the payments. Another defense attorney, in describing the video during cross-examination, said Kamara was “thrusting” the cash in his client’s hand without White requesting it. Prosecutors argued that White, after taking the cash payments, didn’t attempt to return the cash and agreed to “get to work” on Kamara’s behalf.

Video of the pair’s final meeting on Aug. 18, 2024, shows them discussing another potential future business opportunity in federal contracting, an area White said he was interested in pursuing.

“I don’t know how long I’m going to do politics,” he mused, adding that he was thinking about how he could set up additional streams of income.

As White exited Kamara’s car, the two men turned to more light-hearted fare, discussing plans to have some fun together — maybe going on a trip to the Dominican Republic or Colombia.

Then, a new voice can be heard in the video, yelling at White: “Put your hands up.”

Suddenly, White was surrounded by federal agents. He was under arrest.

entries.title: Families of 67 People Who Died in D.C. Midair Collision Want Reform
entries.summary: Several of the victims' families joined with lawmakers and the head of the National Transportation Safety Board outside the Capitol to demand action.
entries.content:
By Josh Funk

The loved ones of the 67 people who died last year when an airliner and Army helicopter collided over Washington, D.C., urged Congress and regulators Tuesday to do more now so other families aren't left clutching belongings and memories instead of their spouses and children.

Several of the victims' families joined with top lawmakers and the head of the National Transportation Safety Board outside the U.S. Capitol to demand action, but it may be difficult for this Congress to pass anything ahead of the midterm elections. And lawmakers are still trying to draft a compromise bill that will combine elements of the competing proposals that previously passed the House and Senate.

Doug Lane said he has the U.S. figure skating jacket that his son Spencer worked so hard to earn and pieces of his wife Christine's laptop that were retrieved from the wreckage after their plane plunged into the icy Potomac River in the deadliest U.S. aviation disaster since 2001. Everyone aboard was killed when American Airlines Flight 5342 from Wichita, Kansas, and the Army Black Hawk helicopter on a training mission collided. The victims included 28 members of the figure skating community.

Lane said the families don't want to see the key reforms recommended after this crash — which include requiring planes to be equipped with systems that will let pilots know exactly where other aircraft are — to wind up like some of the never-implemented measures proposed after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. Airline pilots are still pushing for secondary barriers to keep someone from storming the cockpit when the door is opened.

“That is what fading urgency looks like. Something everyone agrees will make people safer gets caught in process, objections, exceptions and delay until you look up and an entire generation has passed. Flight 5342 cannot follow that path,” Lane said.

The FAA quickly restricted helicopter traffic around Reagan National Airport when it became clear that a helicopter route in the approach path of the airport's secondary runway didn’t ensure enough separation between helicopters and planes. But the NTSB remains unsatisfied with the FAA's response to a third of the 33 safety recommendations it received.

FAA Administrator Brian Bedford testified on Capitol Hill Tuesday that his staff will work to address those concerns, but he also needs guidance from Congress.

Already, steps have been taken to prevent helicopters and planes from sharing the same airspace around Reagan airport, and air traffic controllers are now prohibited from relying only on pilots to see other aircraft and avoid them.

But concerning incidents continue to happen, such as when an airline jet was allowed to take off just as President Donald Trump's helicopter was taking off from the White House last month.

Lane and many other victims' families traveled to the nation's capital time after time in the 595 days since the crash.

“We can tell them stories, we can ask questions. We can push for answers. We can take action. That’s the work that belongs to us. But we cannot do anybody else’s work for them,” Lane said. “We need the people with the power to turn this tragedy into change to do theirs and to finish it.”

Senators Ted Cruz and Maria Cantwell and NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said it would be a shame to reach the second anniversary of the crash, without Congress passing the reforms her agency recommended, nor the Federal Aviation Administration and Defense Department making more safety improvements. Cruz said he hopes Congress will be able to pass a bill during the lame duck session that will follow November's elections.

Rachel Feres, who lost her cousin and his wife and two young daughters in the crash, said she can’t believe there's still debate about whether pilots transporting hundreds of passengers should have the best collision-avoidance technology available, when most modern cars come equipped with arrays of sensors to check blind spots and even apply the brakes in an emergency.

Feres and the other families have been surprised at the amount of lobbying against requiring all planes flying in crowded airspace to be equipped with existing technology that can help pilots know the location of all other aircraft flying nearby. Homendy has said those ADS-B In systems would have prevented this crash. Some airlines have endorsed them, but cost concerns from other airlines and private plane owners have been a stumbling block.

The airlines have the money and power to get this done, Feres said. “This is not about whether you can afford to act … you have the leverage, you have the voice. The question is why safety so rarely gets the same urgency as the next quarterly earnings report.”

“Do the thing you would demand if your wife and son were on that airplane. Do what you would do if your granddaughter was traveling home with her teddy bear. You know how to move fast when money is on the line. Move fast when lives are,” Feres said.

But some airlines have already begun to add the technology to their planes, partly because in addition to the safety benefits, the systems can help increase the number of planes that can fly into an airport by spacing them more precisely. American Airlines leads the industry, having added the technology to its Airbus A321s over the past several years, equipping more than 300 of its roughly 1,000 planes to date. But the systems aren't yet standard equipment on all planes.

Roughly three quarters of the pilots of business jets and smaller single-engine Cessnas and Bonanzas use portable devices that only cost $400. They can tap into this location data and display the information about nearby aircraft on an iPad.

The safety reform bills stalled earlier this year when the narrower Senate bill came up one vote short in the House after the military reversed course and opposed it at the last minute. And lawmakers have had trouble reconciling the Senate bill with the more comprehensive House version that took a different approach on several key points.

Homendy said the victims' families deserve to see more action.

“We can’t spend another moment looking them in the eye and doing nothing. We have to. We have an obligation,” Homendy said. “We owe it to these families. We owe it to passengers. We owe it to the traveling public. We owe it to cargo pilots and so much more to improve safety now.”

Associated Press writer Hannah Fingerhut in Des Moines, Iowa, contributed.

entries.title: Trump Administration Approves Sending Powerful Bombs to Israel in $2.8 Billion Weapons Sale
entries.summary: The proposed sale comes as Israel faces increasing international isolation over its war in Gaza.
entries.content:
By Michelle L. Price and Matthew Lee

The Trump administration is planning to deliver powerful 2,000-pound bombs to Israel as part of an upcoming arms deal, weapons that prompted such concerns about the possibility of mass casualties in Gaza that the Biden administration paused their delivery two years ago.

The $2.8 billion package includes 40,000 of the bombs, made up of 20,000 Mk84s and 20,000 BLU-117s, according to two U.S. officials and a person familiar with the plan who spoke Tuesday on condition of anonymity to discuss the package, which is not yet final.

Congress has been informally notified about the pending deal, most of which is to be paid for with foreign military financing — in which U.S. taxpayer dollars are given to Israel to turn around and buy the weapons from the United States.

The proposed sale is just the latest in a series of Trump administration steps to improve Israeli’s military capacity. The conflict in Gaza has left tens of thousands of Palestinians dead and has decimated the enclave. The U.S. brokered a fragile ceasefire, but violence has continued.

The package, which was reported earlier by The Washington Post, comes as Israel has faced increasing international isolation over its war in Gaza in response to the deadly Oct. 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas.

The sale signals that some strains in the relationship between President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, especially since the two countries launched the war against Iran in February, are not impeding the closeness of the U.S.-Israeli alliance. Trump has had a hot-and-cold history with Netanyahu over the years and expressed some frustration with Netanyahu tied to the Iran conflict before their latest meeting in July at the White House.

In 2024, the Biden administration held off on one shipment of the bombs, but Trump lifted that hold when he took office again.

Last year, the Trump administration bypassed a normal congressional review process and approved a nearly $3 billion sale to Israel that included more than 35,500 of the bombs. The administration then approved a new series of arms sales to Israel totaling $6.67 billion in January.

The 2,000-pound bombs have multiple variants, with some designed to penetrate deep, underground targets while others detonate above ground and cause widespread damage.

Though the Israeli military has offered few details about what bombs and artillery it has used in Gaza, experts analyzing strike footage and blast fragments found on-site believe the U.S.-made bombs have been used there, targeting a tunnel network used by Hamas but also killing of people in densely populated areas.

While the heaviest fighting in Gaza has subsided since the fragile ceasefire took hold in October, Israel has continued to carry out strikes in the territory, including some overnight and into Tuesday that killed several people. That is even after Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and a key Mideast negotiator, met with Netanyahu last month in an effort to push the ceasefire deal forward and asked Israel to reduce its attacks.

Militants have carried out shooting attacks on Israeli troops, and Israel says its strikes are in response to those and other ceasefire violations.

The Hamas-led attack on southern Israel in 2023 killed around 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostage. Israel’s offensive in Gaza to retaliate has killed more than 73,264 Palestinians, including those killed since the ceasefire, Gaza’s Health Ministry said.

entries.title: The FBI Says It Thwarted a Russian Plot to Kill a Prominent Dissident in D.C.
entries.summary: Authorities say Russian intel services are planning to kill individuals in the U.S. and Europe.
entries.content:
By Larry Neumeister

NEW YORK — The intelligence services of the Russian Federation are plotting to carry out targeted killings in the U.S. and in European nations supporting Ukraine, federal authorities said Tuesday in announcing they'd thwarted a plot to kill a prominent Russian dissident believed to be living in Washington, D.C.

Five people assumed to be living abroad were charged in the plot, according to an indictment unsealed in Manhattan federal court. It said a network of the Russian intelligence services has paid and tried to pay individuals in the United States and in other countries since 2024 to surveil and then kill Russian dissidents.

The associates recruited by the network also have been solicited to carry out acts of terrorism against civilian and military infrastructure in European countries that are perceived to be aligned with Ukraine, the indictment said.

James C. Barnacle Jr., head of New York's FBI office, said the agency disrupted the plans “through relentless work” as members of the intelligence services and their affiliates "conspired to intimidate, threaten, or murder people on U.S. soil and around the world.”

Darren B. Cox, head of the Washington, D.C., office of the FBI, in a release cited “extraordinary work by multiple FBI field offices, components, and partner agencies" and said they “moved quickly to disrupt the plot."

According to the release, a network of people working for the Russian Federation's intelligence services had since at least 2024 conspired to conduct and had conducted attacks and murders around the world, including within the United States.

Previously the network had focused on Russian dissidents and defectors but following Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine had targeted nations perceived to be allies of Ukraine, the release said. Recently, members of the network have tried to recruit multiple people in the United States, it said.

U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said in the release that the Russian-led network said the people charged in the foiled plot “conspired to cause destruction and mayhem around the world, including right here in the United States.”

Among those charged in the indictment were three high-ranking members of the Russian intelligence services, authorities said. They were identified as Yuri Khrameev, a former colonel in the Russian intelligence services; his son, Kirill Khrameev, an officer in the Federal Security Service of Russia; and Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, a Cuban national and an influential member of the Cuban diaspora living in Russia.

The indictment said the Federal Security Service is Russia’s principal security agency and the successor agency to the former Soviet Union’s Committee for State Security, which was known as the KGB.

Yuri Khrameev and two others charged in the indictment — Yaidel Delgado Suarez and Angel Eduardo Castro, both living in Russia — recruited a Venezuelan citizen living in Brooklyn to surveil and murder a prominent Russian dissident they believed to be residing in Washington, D.C., the indictment said.

It said the Brooklyn resident was sent to two locations associated with the targeted victim and was given “explicit instructions on how to conduct surveillance” while being promised $1,000 and $1,500 to carry out the work.

After conducting the surveillance and providing multiple photographs and videos of locations associated with the intended victim, the U.S. resident turned down the $40,000 that was offered to “eliminate” or “disappear” the target through murder, authorities said.

When the offer was rejected, the member of the intelligence services who made it offered multiple other people within the United States substantial amounts of money to finish the job, the indictment said.

entries.title: Democrats’ Gavel Race Heats Up on House Small Business Committee
entries.summary: The longtime top Democrat on the committee is stepping down, so Reps. Gil Cisneros and Sharice Davids will likely battle it out for the top job.
entries.content:
Rep. Gil Cisneros is running for the top Democratic slot on the House Small Business Committee, he announced Wednesday, launching a bid to replace retiring Rep. Nydia Velázquez, who held the position for nearly three decades.

Velázquez said in November that she was retiring from office because it was time for “a new generation of leaders to step forward.” The New York congresswoman has served as the top Democrat on the committee since 1998.

“We are experiencing a period of instability and economic uncertainty spurred by a self-motivated President who doesn’t care about Americans’ financial situation,” Cisneros wrote in a Dear Colleague letter, first shared with The Washington Sun. “Now is the time for a focused, aggressive, and forward-looking strategy that puts our small businesses first.”

The California congressman is the first Democrat to officially throw his hat in the ring for the position. Rep. Sharice Davids of Kansas is considering running for the position as well, according to a person familiar with her thinking. Punchbowl News first reported that Davids was eyeing a run.

Davids is currently not a member of the Small Business Committee, so it’s unclear if she would need to get permission from the House Democratic Steering and Policy Committee in order to participate. According to the House Democratic Caucus rules, only committee members can run for chair. She served on the Small Business Committee from 2019 to 2025.

“It’s new that people who aren’t even on the committee [are] running to chair it,” one Steering Committee member told The Sun, though others have jumped to leader roles from other panels before.

With House Democrats hoping to win the majority in November, Cisneros told The Sun the Small Business Committee needed to increase its oversight of the Trump administration.

“We’ve only had the [Small Business Administration] administrator come and testify one time over the last two years,” Cisneros said. “This whole committee this whole time has just been really just a pat on the back to the Trump administration, right? When, at the same time, all we’re hearing is that the instability is causing chaos among small businesses.”

Cisneros, who was a small business owner, said that as chair of the committee, he’d like to have more hearings with SBA officials.

“We want to question them all. We want them to come to explain themselves and try and justify decisions that they're making, ” Cisneros added. “None of that is happening right now.”

THE LATEST

It was either a case of “brazen bribery,” or one built on an untrustworthy informant who “needed a get-out-of-jail card.”

Those were the two divergent arguments made by prosecutors and defense attorneys Tuesday during the first day of Ward 8 council member Trayon White’s trial on federal bribery charges, reports The Washington Sun’s Jenny Gathright.

For the prosecution, the case is simple: White accepted envelopes full of cash from D.C. businessman Allieu Kamara in exchange for promises to help him keep and land more lucrative contracts with the city. Prosecutor John Crabb Jr. says White was “selling his office as a D.C. Council member” for a North Carolina real estate venture he hoped to get in on — and because “it’s really expensive to see girls and have fun.”



For the defense, though, the only simple truth is that White was set up by the government, which relied on Kamara — who defense attorney Warren Gary Kohlman called “corrupt to the bone.” He also contended that even if White pocketed the cash, he didn’t do anything official to help Kamara. “If there is no quid pro quo … it is not bribery,” he argued.

The trial also provided deeper insights into White himself, a three-term lawmaker raised in Ward 8. In videos shown to jurors of White and Kamara discussing businesses in a car, White shared how the stresses of his job and his repeated exposure to death had driven him to therapy.

Also in the courtroom were family, friends and other supporters of White’s, there in solidarity. “Good luck,” one supporter told a grateful White in the court hallway. “We love you. The whole city loves you.” At the same time and mere blocks away, his council colleagues were kicking back into session — without him, for now.

White’s trial is expected to last two weeks. While he’s not expected to testify, he did share his thoughts in an Instagram post after court ended for the day: “Still standing tall. Love y’all.”





DEEP DIVE

Washington Spirit Moms (7741x5160, AR: 1.50)
Andi Sullivan, Ashley Hatch and Aubrey Kingsbury are the longest-tenured members of the Washington Spirit, weathering nine seasons of change together on the NWSL team’s roster. They’re now experiencing one more big change together: All are first-time mothers.

They’re part of a baby boom on the Spirit, joined by veteran defender Casey Krueger, who gave birth to her second child this year. Their babies have become familiar presences both at the team training facility and on the road, writes The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri. Thanks to an NWSL policy allowing players to designate a child care provider who can travel with the team, new mothers in the league do not have to make tough choices between playing and parenting. They can instead simply integrate their new lives into their old ones.

It has been a transformative benefit for the mothers and a source of delight for their teammates, some of whom jokingly refer to the team’s “emotional support babies.” It’s also been a unique experience for the children themselves, who are getting doted on by other players, meeting all sorts of soccer icons and traveling the country.





FROM THE DISTRICT

The Kennedy Center Board of Trustees voted Tuesday to temporarily shutter the institution’s main building after repeated requests by President Donald Trump, who claims the performing arts center “is in a virtual state of collapse,” The Sun’s Jenna Monnin reports.

It’s unclear whether the renovation — expected to cost $250 million — will happen. Trump said the construction would not proceed unless he is allowed to add his name to the building, a response to a federal court ruling earlier Tuesday that blocked the board from affixing his name to the building without congressional approval, The Sun’s Angie Orellana Hernandez reports.

Howard University has begun a national search for its 19th president, who will helm the school at a fraught moment. Howard made headlines this summer over its decision to unenroll 502 incoming freshmen — though at least 200 were ultimately reinstated.

More D.C. families are struggling to put food on the table than at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, due to the climbing cost of living and cuts to federal assistance, reports The Sun’s Kendall Staton.

A new lawsuit claims that D.C. jail staff did nothing when a person incarcerated in the mental health unit set a series of fires that allegedly caused others lasting respiratory damage and psychological distress, The Washington Post reports.

The National Zoo will soon be home to the only Arabian leopards outside of the Arabian Peninsula, Axios D.C. reports. The zoo broke ground yesterday on a $51.6 million habitat for the critically endangered cats, which are expected to arrive in D.C. in 2028 for a 2029 exhibit opening.

A legal battle over the National Guard’s presence in D.C. is playing out in South Carolina. The Post and Courier newspaper reports that the state’s Supreme Court heard arguments Tuesday in a lawsuit filed by the state chapter of the ACLU, which argued that Republican Gov. Henry McMaster unlawfully deployed South Carolina troops to D.C. at Trump’s behest. There are currently 3,120 National Guard troops in D.C. from 19 states; South Carolina is contributing only 20 as of this week.

For salseros and salseras: Salsa Dancing on the Waterfront at The Wharf, Thursdays through Oct. 8.

For the Odyssey-obsessed: Gods, Goddesses and Lotus Eaters: A Hirshhorn Odyssey, Friday.

For city lovers: H Street Festival, Saturday.

For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here.





SPORTS

The Mystics will play a game tomorrow for the first time in 20 days, following a rare midseason hiatus around the FIBA World Cup. The Sun’s Alex Schiffer reports that all three Washington players who took part in the international tournament — Sonia Citron, Kiki Iriafen and Alicia Florez — will suit up Thursday and play without restrictions. The Mystics, sitting seventh in the WNBA standings with four regular-season games remaining, will look to regain some momentum after winning five of their final seven games before the break.

Caps star Alex Ovechkin is drawing blowback on social media this week after appearing in a campaign ad for the United Russia party in support of President Vladimir Putin, Schiffer reports. Celebrity chef José Andrés, a Caps fan, called it a “sad day for my beloved DC team.”

entries.title: Hoaxes Are Back
entries.content:
Today’s notice: The shifting politics of AI meet the stubborn politics of MAGA. Auditing the White House “Fraud Ledger.” A Democrat gets her dad to tell South Carolina she’s not a socialist. Trump’s going to Ohio. House gavel goss. And: North Carolina Republicans are excited to see the president.





THE LATEST

Third time’s the charm? “Every Democrat senator suddenly races to a microphone to talk about AI after being eerily silent for months and months and months,” Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters in the Rose Garden yesterday afternoon. “So to talk about the timing of this as being nothing but an effort to influence the midterms, I shouldn’t have to say that out loud.”

Call it the soft-sell “Democrat hoax” talking point, which Donald Trump’s administration has tried in vain to make stick a couple times in the second term. The Epstein files issue, which was so popular among Trump’s base that it helped get him reelected, was briefly refashioned as a “Democrat hoax” when it started to spin out of control in Congress. That did not end awesomely for team White House. Recently, Trump tried to cast 2026 affordability politics as a hoax. To see how well that went, one only need look to his subsequent pivot to vaporware $5,000 checks as a campaign closer. Not a very subtle acknowledgement that every voter cares about money this cycle.

To see how well the strategy might work on the rapidly shifting politics of AI, journey with The Washington Sun’s Manuela Silva across town yesterday at just about the same time Blanche was making his case. The Pro-Human Assembly conference brought together a collection of pro-AI-regulation voices who were very recently dismissed as wearing tinfoil hats when it comes to AI. Now everyone’s interested in their headwear. (For the record, the actual hats popular at the conference said “Pro-Human” on them.)

“Even two months ago I was describing myself as a lone voice on the existential risk of artificial intelligence, and now it’s not lone at all,” Rep. Don Beyer (D-Virginia), one speaker at the conference and a co-chair of the Congressional Artificial Intelligence Caucus, told Manuela. “It’s nice.”

The politics on display at the conference were certainly not mainstream Democratic. Or mainstream anything, really. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) and Trump ally Steve Bannon spoke back to back on stage. “They’re both human, and they both want the future with humans in charge,” explained attendee Max Tegmark, a founder of the Future of Life Institute. Try finding the partisan message in that statement.

The AI issue rallies elements of Trump’s base as much as anyone else’s. “This is nothing new to me,” former Tea Party luminary Amy Kremer told The Sun’s Jasmine Wright on C-SPAN of the sudden turn to AI regulation this month. She’s another of the AI tinfoil-hat wearers suddenly feeling seen: “I think the story is that it’s actually out there in the public and people are talking about it.” She wants Trump to embrace government oversight of AI.

Speaking of base politics, 2028 Democrats are also trying to find a lane. The Sun’s Elena Schneider, Alex Roarty and Jeff Stein report on the scramble among expected candidates to place that tinfoil hat just so. “Until this week, the incentives were to say nothing. If you said something, Big Tech would come in and kill you, and if you said nothing, it was safer,” Democratic strategist Rob Flaherty told The Sun. “The mood went from ‘Don’t make any sudden moves’ to ‘You need to be proactive on AI.’”

FROM THE WHITE HOUSE


“Fraud Ledger” is a fraud? The White House website lists what the Trump administration calls its successes in its war on fraud in government programs, but it’s riddled with misleading claims, experts tell The Sun’s Natalie Alms. The site includes an agency-by-agency list of fraud detected, prevented and clawed back, although it only offers basic definitions for those claims, including JD Vance’s assertion from the Dallas convention stage that the administration has uncovered nearly $250 billion in fraud using data analytics to find anomalies.

“No idea how this can be legitimate,” said a current senior official from an inspector general’s office.

FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


First on The Sun: Democrats go on air in South Carolina Senate race. A seven-figure TV ad buy from Annie Andrews’ campaign starts today with two spots, our Christa Dutton learned. One focuses on the Democratic nominee’s career as a pediatrician and the cost of health care. The other, far more fun one features Andrews’ Republican father telling South Carolinians, “Look, Annie’s not some crazy socialist.”

Scoop: Trump to campaign in Ohio. The president is expected to stump in Ohio in the coming weeks, according to two sources familiar with his plans, our Kadia Goba reports. The visit comes after Fox polling found 51% of Ohio voters are concerned that Republican Sen. Jon Husted is too close to the president.

FROM A POTENTIAL FUTURE


It’s gavel-scrappin’ time for House Democrats. If they win the House majority, Democrats will have a lot of committee chairs to dole out. The campaigning has begun. The Sun’s Oriana González reports on the nascent fight for the House Small Business Committee gavel. Veteran Rep. Nydia Velázquez (D-New York), who has been the top member of her party on the committee for a long time, is retiring. Oriana learned that Rep. Gil Cisneros (D-California) is running to replace her, potentially pitting him against Rep. Sharice Davids (D-Kansas), who is also considering a run.

Join us for the livestream of The American Small Business Summit. Featuring Jamie Dimon (JPMorganChase), Rep. Tune in for today’s livestream on YouTube.

Programming from 3:30 – 5:00 p.m. ET

Event presented by JPMorganChase. 





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Carolina on Trump’s mind. The president travels to North Carolina today for the first time since December. That trip was all about boosting close ally Michael Whatley’s campaign for Senate — and so is this one, The Sun’s Christa Dutton reports. Whatley is lagging in general election fundraising and polls, and his allies hope Trump can light a fire under voters. Kevin Leebrick, a small business owner in North Carolina who isn’t registered with a party but donated to Whatley’s campaign last summer, said he’s “cautiously optimistic that we get [the race] turned around.”

entries.title: Surging AI Fears Are Scrambling the Early 2028 Campaign
entries.summary: Democrats are getting busy. “The mood went from, ‘don’t make any sudden moves,’ to ‘you need to be proactive,’” said Rob Flaherty.
entries.content:
Potential Democratic presidential candidates are scrambling to carve out their own lanes on artificial intelligence with renewed urgency, after months of laying low got blown up by last week's spike in apocalyptic angst.

Possible 2028 candidates and their top staffers have sought advice from both Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), who wants Democrats to back a temporary pause on AI development, and New York State Assembly member Alex Bores, who launched his own AI safety group this week, according to three people familiar with these private conversations. Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, a potential candidate, discussed AI regulations with Rep. Bill Foster (D-Illinois) at the Illinois Democratic Party dinner last week, according to a person familiar with the interaction.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who is also eyeing a 2028 campaign, could push for more legislative action in his state after signing an AI safety bill this summer, according to a person familiar with the governor’s thinking. On Thursday, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro is scheduled to give an AI-focused speech in Pittsburgh.

A flurry of memos started circulating among Democrats this week, as strategists sought further messaging guidance ahead of the midterms. One poll that made the rounds, obtained by The Washington Sun, found 60 percent of Americans believe the government should slow down AI development to make sure it’s safe, even if that meant China would catch up. The poll, conducted by Blue Rose Research for the Center for Shared AI Prosperity, found a majority of voters wanted to “pause development” of AI until “stronger safeguards exist.”

The AI-focused blitz, from advice-seeking to message-framing research, is a marked departure for the potential 2028 candidates. For much of the last year, those same Democrats largely avoided weighing in on AI-related issues. In some cases, potential 2028 candidates have reversed course after initially leaning into more pro-AI positions around data center construction.

Democratic operatives now expect AI to dominate the 2028 primary debate, and the factions are starting to materialize.

“I’ve been getting calls from 2028 teams saying, ‘What the fuck should I do?’” said Rob Flaherty, an alum of Kamala Harris’ 2024 presidential campaign who recently launched a super PAC, Tomorrow Together, to advise Democrats on AI policy. “Until this week, the incentives were to say nothing. If you said something, Big Tech would come in and kill you, and if you said nothing, it was safer. The mood went from, ‘don’t make any sudden moves,’ to ‘you need to be proactive on AI.’”

AI exploded into the political conversation over the last week, after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon publicly quit his job and said his former employer was “gambling with our lives.” His viral post triggered a cascade of responses, including an unprecedented call from the leaders of Anthropic and other AI companies for increased federal regulation and a slowdown in development. All these moves come just weeks after OpenAI acknowledged its AI agents went rogue and hacked into rival AI start-up Hugging Face.

“The people who are thinking of running for president realize how important this issue is and are doing all they can to get up to speed on it as quickly as possible, and because it changes so quickly, this isn't something you can just cram for or study once,” Bores said. “This is an ongoing conversation, so I expect to have those continue and any way that we can help any of the potential Democratic nominees, we stand ready to help.”
JB Pritzker AP - 25245753472865 (5520x3680, AR: 1.50)Interviews with six advisers to potential 2028 candidates, who were granted anonymity to describe private discussions, said there are several concerns about AI, including a lack of knowledge about the technology and theoretical job losses, making it less clear what the best policy prescriptions might be. Others said the blockbuster political spending from AI-backed super PACs in Democratic primaries had a chilling effect on Democratic candidates pushing on the issue, both in 2026 and ahead of 2028.

“A lot of candidates have a default desire to tread carefully because the technology is so fast-moving, they don’t want to seem like a Luddite, and they also fear making an enemy out of an industry with deep pockets,” said one 2028 adviser, who pointed to the fact that most potential 2028 candidates have not joined Sanders in calling for a moratorium on AI. “But there’s a real opening for a candidate to stand out if they are willing to err on the side of being aggressive.”

Over the last week, Pritzker said it’s “time to sound the alarm” on AI, urging federal action, as did Shapiro. California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a landmark child safety bill. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who wrote in June 2025 that “we are still underreacting on AI,” said it’s “deeply dangerous” for Congress to “sit on its hands.” Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona) said “not taking action on AI now is just plain dumb,” referring to President Donald Trump’s rejection of AI guardrails. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) called out the “tech lords” for not going “far enough” and argued for a “pause” on “recursive self improving AI.”

So far, there is a coalescing “consensus on values and posture, but not yet on how that translates into specific regulatory policy,” said one Democratic strategist involved in the discussions around AI and 2028. “The CEOs opened the door for that consolidation because the industry is signaling they’re open to it.”

But some divisions are emerging. Harris drew sharp criticism after praising a new effort, led by Democratic megadonor Ron Conway, to improve the relationship between Democrats and the AI industry, arguing the party needed to find a way to regulate AI “without sacrificing the technology’s benefits.”

“The problem is the outsized influence of the industry,” tweeted Democratic strategist Morris Katz, who called Harris’ tweet a “total misread.”

“Take them on,” he posted. “Don’t serve as an accomplice.”
Kamala Harris AP - 26208746709571 (4000x2667, AR: 1.50)Potential candidates have a range of ready-made options at their disposal for responding to voter angst. The most moderate ideas already in circulation include limiting state or federal tax breaks for data centers, imposing stricter disclosure of water and electricity usage and creating new programs to retrain workers displaced in the AI transition. Those policies would keep intact the basic structure of AI development.

At the other end of the spectrum are proposals to bring the frontier labs under direct government control or give the government a means to shut them down. Sanders has championed legislation to nationalize the frontier labs by having the government seize a majority of their equity — a step resisted thus far by most Democrats, including all of the potential 2028 candidates.

Democrats are also split over the best way to tax the frontier labs and the data centers that support them. Casar has proposed a tax on “tokens” that would charge AI companies based on how much computing power they use, ensuring that federal revenue rises the more the technology is adopted. Opponents of the idea say such a model would tax consumption, with a higher bill ultimately getting passed onto users.

Sanders’ nationalization plan would theoretically avoid that pitfall, but comes with challenges of its own, including the downside of tying government funding to keeping AI running.

The intensifying alarm in Washington has spurred greater interest in these more dramatic solutions, experts and congressional aides said. But even if potential candidates and their advisers are talking about them behind the scenes, not all are eager to discuss them publicly yet.
DC: Senate Democrats Hold Press Conference on the Dismantlin (6109x4075, AR: 1.50)“Not every presidential candidate wants to take a stance on it,” said one Democratic strategist working on AI politics, who noted that AI wasn’t ever discussed during the last presidential primary in 2020. “I think it is a lot of ‘let’s see what happens over the next couple of weeks.’”

“But the reality is, the conversation about AI regulation is not going to go away,” the strategist said.

Part of what will make AI such a volatile campaign issue is its newness, party strategists said. Candidates have spent decades familiarizing themselves with issues like crime, the economy or culture war but might have learned about ChatGPT or Claude only since the last presidential election.

“I think if 2026 is going to be the midterm of data centers, 2028 is going to be the AI election,” said Ravi Mangla, spokesperson for the progressive Working Families Party. “Any serious candidate for 2028 is going to have a problem breaking out from the crowd without a comprehensive AI platform.”

The WFP earlier this year debuted its own AI policy platform, which called for a federal jobs program to help combat rising unemployment tied to the proliferation of the new technology.

Some strategists said they expect the AI political debate’s focus will soon shift from safety and data centers to job losses, with the potential to become the dominant issue in the presidential primary.

“This issue is designed in a lab to freak voters out,” said Pat Dennis, president of American Bridge, a Democratic super PAC.

“People need to think about skating to where the puck is going,” he said. “And what is going to be tangible to the voter in 2028, at least to me, is it’s almost certainly going to be AI-related job losses and fears around AI job losses.”

entries.title: The White House’s 'Fraud Ledger' Includes Misleading Claims
entries.summary: One senior official within an inspector general’s office questioned whether the public is “being bamboozled.”
entries.content:
The White House is broadcasting its anti-fraud crusade to voters in the leadup to the midterm elections with a “Fraud Ledger” that claims the Trump administration has uncovered hundreds of billions in misused funds.

The Washington Sun’s review of the ledger found that it includes misleading and unsubstantiated claims, and the White House has not provided details about how the administration crunched its fraud numbers. When asked by The Sun, a senior White House official said that the “methodology was produced by fraud experts from within the Task Force and communicated to agencies.”

The absence of details, and the apparent inconsistencies in the numbers, have oversight experts both inside and outside the government questioning the veracity of the White House’s work.

“The fraud ledger appears to be primarily a piece of propaganda that provides very little, if any, meaningful information,” said Linda Miller, president of the government-integrity-focused Program Integrity Alliance who worked at the Government Accountability Office for a decade.

“No idea how this can be legitimate,” a current senior official with an Office of Inspector General said of the White House’s claim that it has uncovered $250 billion in misused federal funds.

“If they’re not giving their methodology, these are kind of useless numbers,” the official said. “How is this at all serious?”

The Trump administration has made the anti-fraud task force, created in March and led by Vice President JD Vance, a central part of its political messaging. The administration has pointed to fraud as it’s held up billions in Medicaid funding in Minnesota and California — a move that has put California’s at-home care program at risk for cuts, as The Sun has reported previously.

The White House’s ledger, published in August, includes an agency-by-agency list of fraud detected, prevented and clawed back. It does not offer details about how agencies calculated those numbers.

It’s indisputable that some amount of fraud exists in government programs, especially pandemic-era policies that federal agencies rushed to get off the ground to respond to the crisis. But the numbers on the ledger and the administration’s rhetoric around its fraud work overstate what the task force has accomplished.

Vance cited one data point from the website last week at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention, telling the crowd that “we found $250 billion of fraud just since the president made me the fraud czar.”

The ledger says the administration uncovered $245.7 billion in fraud — but it cites January 2025 as the start date, well before Vance was tapped to lead the work in April of this year. The White House did not clarify which time frame is correct.

Asked about how the White House calculated the number being touted by Vance, the senior White House official told The Sun that “fraud uncovered values are reported from the agencies and are data-driven calculations of misspent funds.” Typically, oversight officials have to investigate anomalies flagged during data analyses to weed out false positives. The White House did not clarify if and how agencies are doing so.

The senior White House official, who spoke only on the condition of anonymity, pointed to the Small Business Administration’s identification of $22.2 billion in suspected fraudulent loans as an example of fraud the Trump administration has uncovered.

But those loans were tagged as potentially fraudulent during the Biden administration, the SBA itself said in April when it announced it was referring them to the Treasury Department to recoup, an action also listed on the White House website.

The website says the SBA has recovered a total of $22.6 billion.

If the $22.2 billion referral to Treasury is included there, “then nearly all of the headline SBA enforcement number represents debt sent for collection rather than money already recovered,” Miller wrote in a recent blog post detailing her efforts to verify the SBA’s claims on the White House website.

The SBA didn’t respond to request for comment.

The ledger also lists the capture of four fugitives as a “top ten” anti-fraud action by the Trump administration in a blurb touting $5.4 billion in "intended loss charged.” Three were charged before the current administration took office, in 2019 and 2024.

The White House did not clarify if those schemes were included in the $5.4 billion in intended loss charged or why they are included on a page of fraud “identified” since January 2025.

The White House says it is saving $62 million annually in its fight against fraud by decertifying and withholding funding from the main law enforcement entities tasked with rooting out bad actors in Medicaid in Hawaii and New York.

The Trump administration cited poor performance for the Medicaid fraud control unit in Hawaii when it denied its recertification request this summer. It pointed to New York’s strategy to focus on high-impact, complex cases as rational for taking the funding of that office, saying the state was neglecting the other work assigned to the unit, such as patient abuse.

The New York office has recovered over $627 million through fraud investigations since 2019, New York Attorney General Letitia James said at the time, calling the move a “political distraction” that only benefits bad actors.

“I don't even know what to say,” said Andy Schneider, who was a senior advisor at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services during the Obama administration, where he focused on Medicaid program integrity.

“It’s illogical,” Schneider, who is now a research professor at Georgetown University, said of defunding law enforcement units.

Bob Westbrooks, who worked for decades in various inspector general offices until 2022, cautioned that “any savings you might enjoy from not spending federal funds on enforcement are going to be offset by losses” from fraudsters.

The same day the Department of Health and Human Services’ inspector general decertified Hawaii’s unit, the state announced it had tapped a lawyer who defended Trump during 2020 impeachment hearings, Michael Purpura, to lead a new strike force focused on Medicaid fraud.

The White House claims that the Trump administration has stopped $46.2 billion in fraud annually through administrative actions like rule changes. Asked for details about the methodology behind that claim, the White House official told The Sun that its list of “fraud stopped” is “spending averted due to anti-fraud actions.”

The White House’s website includes a “fraud tracker” for individuals to look up a “map of enforcement actions, suspensions, and recoveries by state and locality,” though the interactive feature only lists agencies in Washington, D.C.
fraud map (2094x1208, AR: 1.73)Putting a number on how much fraud has been thwarted by the government is difficult to do accurately, said Mark Greenblatt, a former inspector general at the Interior Department.

“The IG community struggled for years to figure out a metric for determining or quantifying the preventative value of our work,” he told The Sun. “We could never come up with a fair assessment that withstood scrutiny.”

Greenblatt is one of nearly 20 inspectors general Trump has fired since returning to the White House last year and transforming the system the government already had in place to catch waste, fraud and abuse, as The Sun has previously reported.

Experts say the White House’s political approach to the problem risks undermining the administration’s anti-fraud work and eroding the public’s trust.

“Increasing public awareness of fraud and publicizing bona fide enforcement results is in all of our best interests,” Westbrooks said. “These efforts are undermined when the data cannot be verified and enforcement is viewed as selective or politically motivated.”

The current senior OIG official said agency watchdogs should actually consider examining the Trump administration's claims about fraud.

“Is Congress being bamboozled?” they asked. “Is the public being bamboozled?”

entries.title: The Spirit’s New Moms Navigate the Season with Babies in Tow
entries.summary: A league policy allows players to have their babies — and in some cases, their spouses — travel with the team.
entries.content:
Ashley Hatch was on a work trip when her baby started crawling.

The Washington Spirit forward had a match in Los Angeles, more than 2,000 miles from home, when 7-month-old Leo was graduating from a shuffling, haphazard scoot into a full crawl. But that was no problem: Leo was on the road with her, and so was her husband, Jeff. They shared the milestone as a family. And so did the rest of the Spirit, with players and staff crowding around, putting cups down on the floor to create a miniature obstacle course for the baby. Hatch felt her heart swell.

“It’s really cool to see other people love your child,” says Hatch, 31. “I feel really lucky.”

That’s been a theme for the Spirit this season.

Hatch is one of four players who have given birth in the past 15 months, joining Andi Sullivan, Casey Krueger and Aubrey Kingsbury. The babies have come along for the ride as their mothers have worked their way back from maternity leave: An NWSL policy lets them designate a child care provider who can travel with the club at no added cost to the player.

That’s become an essential benefit for the new moms and a source of delight for their teammates. (Some jokingly refer to “emotional support babies.”) As the Spirit push for a return to the NWSL Championship, they’re doing it with a bit less sleep, and a bit more collective maternal love.

“You're so happy for yourself, and then you're so happy for each other,” says Sullivan, who gave birth to a daughter, Millie, in July 2025. “Then you multiply that over and over and over again throughout the team.”
Washington Spirit Moms (7705x5137, AR: 1.50)The experience of motherhood in the league has changed significantly over the past few years. Originally, the NWSL did not have standardized contract protections for maternity leave, and it certainly did not have opportunities for paid child care on the road. With low salaries in a fledgling league, players often felt it would be impossible to plan for a baby while continuing their soccer careers.

“When I first started, there was no chance that I was going to start a family and also try playing,” says Hatch, who entered the league in 2017.

Many of her fellow NWSL players thought similarly. Those who did have children found that accommodations could vary wildly from team to team. But that shifted in 2022, when the NWSL negotiated its first collective bargaining agreement with the Players Association, including a full suite of policies around pregnancy and parenthood.

“I instantly think back to when I first got in the league, and how few mothers there were,” says Krueger, a defender who has played for a decade in the NWSL. “Now, it’s just like you look around, and every team has so many mothers.”

There are, indeed, a record number of moms on league rosters this year: There were 28 at the beginning of the season, and a few more have given birth since. The players say that is not a coincidence.
Spirit Moms, Ashely Hatch (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)Spirit Moms, Casey Krueger (6045x4030, AR: 1.50)Many of them closely watched the example set by the WNBA, which first negotiated a traveling child care provider benefit in 2020, making parenthood feel more accessible to players in that league. As the NWSL grew, the players’ salaries increased and protections expanded, making pregnancy and parenthood feel like a more secure choice. The original collective bargaining agreement from 2022 was renegotiated with added benefits in 2024. It covers everything from guaranteed parental leave to that crucial paid travel for a child care provider.

“How many occupations can you say that mothers get to travel with their kids and do what they love?” Krueger says.

Early motherhood still brings stress, sleep deprivation and scheduling challenges. The return to play is physically taxing and highly variable. But it no longer feels like quite such an existential threat to a pro soccer career.

Krueger is the Spirit’s resident veteran mom. She gave birth to her first child, a boy, in the summer of 2022. When she joined the Spirit in free agency in 2024, so did baby Caleb, coming on road trips along with his nanny.

That felt like a revelation for some younger teammates: They watched up close as Krueger balanced soccer and motherhood. She fit nursing and pumping around training, just like any player might fit a regularly needed task. She allowed them to see that a high chair could be a welcome addition to the occasional team meal. And she kept performing at a high level. In addition to her club play, Krueger is a fixture on the U.S. women’s national soccer team; she gave birth for the first time in between winning bronze at the 2020 Olympics in Tokyo and gold in Paris four years later.

“She was just a huge inspiration to me,” Sullivan says of Krueger. “And there are other incredible moms, both in the league and on the national team, who made it possible even when it was really, really difficult. They turned around and fought to make it easier for us and safer for us, and I think seeing them do that then made me want to do it, too.”

Krueger gave birth to her second child, a daughter named Calla, in March. And she was joined on maternity leave by a trio of first-time moms in Sullivan, Hatch and Kingsbury.
Washington Spirit Moms (7480x4987, AR: 1.50)Spirit Mom, Ashley Hatch (6406x4271, AR: 1.50)Their pregnancies were spaced over the course of a year. (Not intentionally, they are quick to say: “We didn’t plan this at all,” Hatch laughs. “We all just happened to be ready about the same time.”) Sullivan and Hatch have returned to play. Krueger has resumed practicing with the team and is targeting a full return this season. Kingsbury, their veteran goalkeeper, is still on maternity leave after giving birth to son Carter in July, but she has made several appearances at the team training facility, baby in tow.


Just as they’re in slightly different phases of physical recovery, their babies are in slightly different phases of early childhood, which has been an unexpected blessing.

“We help each other every day,” Krueger said. “It’s really cool to have that. Because it can be pretty isolating, so it’s really special to have that here with a group.”

It has been an especially poignant shared experience for Sullivan, Hatch and Kingsbury, navigating motherhood for the first time and doing it together. They are the longest-tenured members of this roster: All three landed on the Spirit during the same week in January 2018. They have watched the club pass through different coaches and owners and facilities. They have won a championship together and lost a championship together. They have supported each other as they have bounced on and off the national team.

Now, after going through so much of their early adulthood together, they are going through one more big life change on the Spirit.

“We've been through a lot,” Sullivan says. “So we've gained a really good understanding of one another. … It’s just a very kind of peaceful thing, because you know you're not the only one, and it's just another way in which we're going through something together.”

Hatch and Sullivan have both designated their husbands as their child care providers for team-related travel. (While men’s soccer culture traditionally has “WAGs,” or wives and girlfriends, they joke about their “HABs,” or husbands and boyfriends.) The benefit has been crucial, they say, especially when it comes to nursing and pumping.

“Getting to bring her, and bring someone to take care of her, is really important,” Sullivan says of having her daughter on road trips. It has been fun, too.

“Before having Leo, Jeff would stay home and I would go on a trip and come back,” Hatch says. “Now, the whole family’s going, and it’s like, wow, this is a little weird.”
Washington Spirit Moms (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)Washington Spirit Moms (7741x5160, AR: 1.50)After a decade of traveling as a pro athlete, she’s realized there was plenty about the experience that she took for granted, but it’s all completely new to her husband. “It makes it exciting,” she says. “It’s just really cool to create those memories together as a family.”

And as a team.

“With Caleb, I always say, like, he doesn't realize how lucky he is,” Krueger says of her firstborn. “The girls show so much support for him, and the same with all the other kids, with Millie, and with Leo, and now with Carter. It's so special to have that many aunties.”

The babies have become much-loved members of the squad. “It just brings a fun energy to everything,” says defender Tara Rudd, who does not have children of her own but hopes to someday.

“Obviously, it makes things so much easier logistically for the mother, but it’s fun for the team, too,” says Rudd, who has long sat in front of Sullivan on the team bus and loves that her seating arrangement now means sitting in front of Millie, her “best friend on the bus.”

Eventually, the mothers say, they can’t wait to explain this to their children. Look at everyone you met. Look at the games you saw. Look at everywhere you went. All before they could walk. Or, as it turns out, right as they started to crawl.
