entries.title: Rep. Tom Kean Jr. Runs Anti-Congressional Stock Trade Mailers As He Trades Stocks
entries.summary: The taxpayer-funded messages don’t mention the New Jersey congressman’s own frequent financial moves.
entries.content:
Rep. Tom Kean Jr. wants his constituents to know: He doesn’t approve of lawmakers trading individual stocks.

In taxpayer-funded mailers sent this month to residents of New Jersey's 7th Congressional District, his office makes clear: “Kean backed legislation to prohibit members of Congress from trading individual stocks.”

Unmentioned in the “public trust”-themed mailer is the fact that Kean ranks among Congress’ most prolific stock traders.

With the aid of financial advisers, Kean has bought or sold individual stocks at least 44 times this year, placing him among the top 10 House lawmakers in terms of individual transactions, according to an analysis of lawmakers’ trades by The Washington Sun.

Kean has traded stocks every single month this year, including throughout the nearly four-month stretch when he disappeared from office with little explanation, according to disclosures made in January, February, March, April, May, June, July and August. Kean later revealed that he underwent treatment for depression during his absence.

The congressman’s stock trades “are initiated and made by third-party advisors with no input from Rep. Kean,” per the disclosures. Each disclosure bears Kean’s digital signature, indicating he is aware of what stocks he owns or that an adviser sold stocks on his behalf.

“I do not direct, influence, approve, or participate in a single investment decision,” Kean said in a statement to The Sun. “I have placed my investable assets in a completely blind structure managed entirely by independent financial professionals, and transactions occur without my input, prior knowledge, or direction. I have held myself to the single highest standard, and I am fighting to hold every politician to a higher standard.”

When Kean first arrived in Congress in 2023, he pledged to put his millions in a “qualified blind trust” — a highly restrictive financial arrangement approved by the House Ethics Committee — but ultimately declined to do so.

As the mailer advertises, Kean “backed legislation to prohibit members of Congress from trading individual stocks.” The Stop Insider Trading Act passed the House in July on a largely party-line vote, with most Democrats arguing the bill did not go far enough to tackle congressional conflicts of interest and the threat of corruption.

The bill would prohibit members of Congress from buying individual stocks in publicly traded companies — in effect barring lawmakers such as Kean from signing off on future stock purchases like the ones that have transformed his portfolio throughout this year.

The mailers Kean sent his constituents are “franked” — a permissible form of communication from members’ offices to constituents using taxpayer funds. Lawmakers often use franked mail to tout their positions or accomplishments ahead of elections.

Franked communications may not, however, contain overt campaign messages, such as requests to oppose an election-season rival. They also may not be sent out less than 60 days before an election; Kean’s mailers were approved 67 days before the midterm election.
Rebecca.Bannett.1 (3500x2333, AR: 1.50)Kean is in a tight race against Democrat and former Navy pilot Rebecca Bennett. Federal records indicate that Bennett sold off her individual stock holdings in 2024.

“My husband and I divested all of our individual stocks, I’m not taking a dime from corporate PACs and I will fight for a full stock trading ban for members of Congress because I want New Jerseyans to know exactly who I serve,” Bennett said in a statement to The Sun.

entries.title: Family of Woman Who Died After Being Denied an Abortion Sues Ken Paxton
entries.summary: The lawsuit states that Tierra Walker, 37, “repeatedly asked for an abortion to save her life” as her health quickly deteriorated.
entries.content:
The family of a 37-year-old woman who died while pregnant filed a lawsuit Tuesday against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and other medical and state actors, alleging that Texas law prevented her from getting an abortion that may have saved her life.

The lawsuit is the first over a death linked to an abortion ban.

Tierra Walker died in 2024 when she was 20 weeks pregnant. The lawsuit states that she “repeatedly asked for an abortion to save her life” as her health quickly deteriorated from a medical condition known as preeclampsia.

“For months, Ms. Walker had been asking for termination of her pregnancy — even though this was a wanted pregnancy — because she did not think she would survive the pregnancy,” the lawsuit filed in Bexar County reads. “Tragically, she was right. An abortion at any point during her pregnancy would have saved her life.”

The court filing alleges that Paxton used his authority as attorney general to “perpetuate a climate of extreme fear throughout the state’s medical community, deliberately ignoring that abortion is the standard of care for many emergent health conditions that arise during pregnancy.”

Paxton has strongly opposed abortion while in office — filing lawsuits over abortion pills, threatening to prosecute doctors who carry out the procedures and defending Texas’ abortion ban in court.

The Republican attorney general is running for U.S. Senate and locked in a close race against Democratic state Rep. James Talarico, who has been a staunch advocate for reinstating abortion protections in the state.

Paxton’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit.

Following the 2022 Supreme Court decision overturning Roe v. Wade, abortions are illegal in Texas with narrow exceptions for pregnant mothers who face life-threatening conditions. The state legislature passed a law in 2025 — one year after Walker’s death — that attempts to clarify when abortions can be performed, but the legislation did not materially expand access to the procedure.

Walker’s family argued that the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio and some of its staff, which were also named in the lawsuit, failed to appropriately screen her or provide life-saving treatment for her serious medical conditions.

“They continued to do nothing even as University Health staff noted that she was ‘at high risk of clinical deterioration and/or death’ and her pregnancy was a ‘barrier’ to her care,” the lawsuit states.

The medical examiner concluded that Walker died of hypertensive cardiovascular disease with superimposed preeclampsia. According to the Cleveland Clinic, preeclampsia is a “serious” blood pressure condition that can develop during pregnancy and can cause organ damage as well as brain injuries.

“The treatment for preeclampsia is immediate delivery — which in Texas before full term is legally an abortion,” the lawsuit states.

The University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio acknowledged The Washington Sun’s request for comment but said it did not have any information to offer at this time.

ProPublica first reported on the details that led to Walker's death in November 2025.

Attorneys for the family described Walker as an “anchor” and said she leaves behind a husband, a disabled mother whom she cared for and a teenage son.

“Ms. Walker was a smart, passionate, ambitious human being. She was an educator with a Teacher of the Year award, a registered dental assistant, and a certified paralegal who constantly strove to educate herself and support her family,” the filing states.

entries.title: House Republican Meeting Turns Into Shouting Match
entries.summary: Speaker Mike Johnson summoned top GOP members to discuss suspending the gas tax, but the session got ugly and personal.
entries.content:
A late-night meeting in House Speaker Mike Johnson’s office went off the rails Tuesday, with multiple sources describing the session as one of the most contentious this year.

“Everyone was fired up,” one source said.

Johnson called a 9:15 p.m. meeting with other members of House Republican leadership. Among those summoned were the top leaders of the five ideological caucuses, known as the “five families,” and some committee chairs.

The speaker wanted to discuss a bill to suspend the gas tax through the election, an effort spearheaded by House Freedom Caucus Chair Andy Harris (R-Maryland). Harris agreed to vote with leaders on a procedural measure in exchange for a commitment. Leaders promised him they would convene a meeting to discuss the possibility of suspending the gas tax.

But the meeting quickly devolved into chaos, according to five sources in the room and another briefed on the meeting.

Rep. Sam Graves (R-Missouri), chair of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, brought in a printed post on X from 2022 in which Harris criticized then-President Joe Biden’s efforts to suspend the gas tax.

“Suspending the federal gas tax is just another Biden Administration stunt to distract from their self-inflicted crisis,” Harris said in the post.

Graves, who sits on a committee of jurisdiction for the gas tax, was opposed to the bill being moved to the floor — outside of regular order — and cited Harris’ previous comments.

Harris got livid and began banging the desk, yelling, “This is fucking war! This is war!” according to sources in the room.

He was starting to storm out of the room when the speaker attempted to stop him by telling him to stay and "talk this out.”

But Rep. Clay Higgins (R-Louisiana), an ally of Harris’, started to berate Graves.

“Why do you have to come at him personally?” Higgins said. “You disrespectful fool!”

He stormed out of the room along with Harris.

The meeting was described by sources as one of the craziest they had ever been part of.

“The room was really tense,” one of the sources said.

The following day, Higgins took to X and fired another shot at Graves, saying in a post that Graves is an “Establishment elitist” who had a “lifetime Heritage score of 69.”

“[Graves] just killed the Freedom Caucus bill that would have canceled the federal fuel tax for 3 months. Our intention was to bring the bill to the House floor tomorrow night. Man wants his taxes,” Higgins said. “And he was rude about it. Unbelievable. The swamp is fighting hard to come back.”

Spokespeople for Higgins, Graves and Harris did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The “dustup,” as one source put it, is just another episode in the chaotic session, with Johnson attempting to govern with a razor-thin margin. Members who view themselves as team players are losing their patience with the same group of colleagues whom they view as too willing to blow everything up to get what they want.

Back in July, Johnson lost his cool when in an argument with Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Florida) and snapped “I’m sick of this shit,” at her. At other times, members such as Reps. Ann Wagner (R-Missouri) and Stephanie Bice (R-Oklahoma) have berated Johnson on the House floor for caving to the demands of the far right at the expense of other members.

All this tension has led to the House routinely canceling votes and sending members home early due to the constant infighting. Less than a day after the contentious meeting, the speaker announced the House was finishing up work early and sending members home until after the midterms.

entries.title: ‘You Can’t Deny It’: Democratic Turnout Has Surged in 2026
entries.summary: Strategists say a combination of rising enthusiasm and a plethora of competitive races helped drive the increase in Senate primaries.
entries.content:
The just concluded primary season made at least one thing resoundingly clear: Democrats are seeing an explosion in voter turnout.

Propelled by a surge in competitive elections and an engaged base, Senate Democratic primaries across the country saw huge spikes in voters this year, according to an analysis of voter participation data from The Washington Sun.

Turnout in these contests rose in 26 of the 30 states that held a Democratic primary this year and were included in the study, compared to their most recent previous race in 2022 or 2024. Five states saw their turnout more than double, while another nine states saw increases of more than 50%.

Across all 30 states, the median increase was about 45% — a figure significant enough that analysts say it’s proof of a national trend rippling through the Democratic Party’s primaries.

“It’s not like just an occasional state where you had this surge in enthusiasm,” said John Couvillon, a Republican pollster who tracks turnout data across the country. “It is occurring regularly and often enough that you can’t deny it.”

https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/lVeVg/10/Maine saw the largest increase, nearly quadrupling its turnout from its 2024 Senate Democratic primary, from about 55,000 votes to 216,000 votes. That spike in isolation is not surprising: The state’s 2024 election was not competitive while the primary race this year featured a contentious battle between Graham Platner and Gov. Janet Mills.

But other states also showed large surges, including Texas (140% increase), Rhode Island (117%), Minnesota (116%) and South Carolina (113%). The increases happened in red and blue states alike, and included some of this year’s top general election battlegrounds, including Iowa, Ohio and North Carolina.

A surge in voter participation isn’t uncommon for a party in the years following a loss in the presidential election — Democrats saw a turnout increase in many of its 2018 primaries during President Donald Trump’s first midterm election. But Democratic strategists say they’re encouraged by the development nonetheless, especially after what many consider a muted initial reaction to Trump’s 2024 victory.

“What you’ve seen over the last three or four months is that delayed response,” said Guy Cecil, a former executive director of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. “More Democrats turning out to vote. More Democrats volunteering. More Democrats participating in the process.”

For the analysis, The Sun compared turnout in 30 Democratic Senate primaries this year to the last Democratic Senate primaries in the state in either 2024 or 2022. The analysis did not include Delaware or South Dakota, which both canceled their Democratic Senate primaries in 2022, or Virginia, which canceled its Senate Democratic primary this year.

The analysis also does not include Alaska, which does not have partisan primaries, or Louisiana, which started holding partisan primaries only this year.

Senate Democrats had more competitive primaries this year than any time in recent memory, featuring battles between the party’s progressive and establishment factions in states like Michigan, Minnesota, Texas and Iowa.

Those battles — which drew millions of dollars in spending and widespread media attention — very likely drove some of the turnout increase, strategists say. Some Republicans contend that intraparty competition is a sign of a divided party and portends poorly for Democrats in November.

“The Democratic Socialists of America have skewed Democrats’ primary turnout,” said Bernadette Breslin, spokesperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee.

Democratic turnout did drop in some states featuring a Senate race this year. That includes Florida, which saw an 18% decline despite a competitive contest. Democrats have suffered difficult defeats in the former battleground state in the Trump era, and Republicans have made significant registration gains that have helped turn the state into a conservative stronghold.

Democratic turnout also dropped in Kansas, which features a competitive race this year. But the state’s comparison is also skewed by a 2022 vote on an abortion amendment to the state’s constitution, which was held on the same day as the state’s Senate primary.

Democratic strategists acknowledge that high primary turnout does not guarantee victories in a general election. But they say the uniform rise in participation is a good indication of voter enthusiasm, which could add as many as a few percentage points to the Democratic candidates’ performance in November.

It’s also not the only metric suggesting the party is in for a strong midterm election.

“When you look at primary turnout and you combine that with special election performance and an increasing gap in the generic ballot, all of these things point to a significant turnout advantage for Democrats,” Cecil said.

Some Senate Democratic primaries saw turnout spikes this year even though they did not feature a competitive race. North Carolina’s primary was mostly ceremonial, featuring an overwhelming favorite in former Gov. Roy Cooper, but still saw a 34% rise in votes compared to the state’s 2022 primary.

Ohio, meanwhile, saw a 55% turnout increase relative to 2024, even though former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown ran as the overwhelming favorite.

Couvillon, the Republican pollster, said his own tracking shows that more Democrats turned out than Republicans in a handful of important battleground states this year, including Wisconsin, Texas, North Carolina, Georgia, Pennsylvania, Michigan and New Hampshire. It is a warning sign for his party.

“Unless you are in a district that is 55% or more Trump, I don’t think a Republican candidate or incumbent can feel entirely secure,” he said. “Because you have this triple whammy of some Republican voters defecting, independents are showing preference for Democrats, and then of course, there’s elevated Democratic enthusiasm.”

entries.title: Bipartisan Frustration That Congress Leaving Key Spy Power Dark Through Elections
entries.summary: “I don’t like FISA being dark an hour,” Sen. James Lankford told The Sun.
entries.content:
Congress is leaving a key surveillance tool dark through the election, a development that is alarming members concerned about new threats stemming from the Iran war and other security issues in the coming months.

The House is planning to adjourn Wednesday until after Election Day, meaning that even if the Senate were to take up a reauthorization of Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), the spy power would remain idle until members return.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune on Tuesday rattled off the to-do list for the three-week session before the chamber breaks for the election sprint, with reupping FISA absent, as Republicans prioritize bills related to overhauling college sports and permitting reform.

The lack of movement is upsetting members who believe it was high time it got done.

“I don’t like FISA being dark an hour,” Sen. James Lankford (R-Oklahoma), a member of the Intelligence Committee, told The Washington Sun. He added that the hard part is “you don’t know what you don’t know. That’s this constant thing that hangs out there all the time. That’s a bad spot for us to be [in] as a country.”

“Going through the 25th anniversary of 9/11, the lesson that we were supposed to learn there is it’s a lot better to be able to find out what’s going to happen before it happens than after,” he added.

Democrats blocked the authority’s reauthorization in June over their concerns about then-acting Director of National Intelligence Bill Pulte but expressed openness to renewing the program after confirming Jay Clayton to the post in August.

Pulte was criticized by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle for his lack of experience and his immediate moves to slash jobs in the intelligence community.

Still, there’s been little rush to renew FISA since the telecommunications companies covered by the law are by and large continuing to cooperate with federal law enforcement agencies. But some lawmakers believe a promise from those companies is not enough to keep the program operating indefinitely without congressional action.

“Fortunately, the telecom companies are continuing to cooperate based on foreign intelligence surveillance court certifications, but that’s going to run out,” said Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), an Intelligence Committee member.

Cornyn also pressed FBI Director Kash Patel about FISA at a hearing on Tuesday, noting that 60% of the president’s daily brief comes from information collected under the authority

“I think we should all be concerned,” Cornyn added.

That worry was shared by Democrats on the panel. Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona) told The Sun he was surprised that the Senate had not yet voted to reauthorize the program since Clayton was installed in early August.

“It’s helpful [the telecom] companies are complying. But there’s always risk until we get the legislation done,” he said.

Lawmakers have debated the issue for months, with critics from both parties calling for more guardrails around the program, which collects data on communications overseas by foreigners who could pose a threat to the U.S. The debate has been particularly contentious in the House –– both chambers earlier in the year passed a temporary extension in order to continue negotiating over provisions that would bolster the law’s privacy protections.

“I think the House is running the least successful legislative operation in House history, and it's going to have a lot of different costs,” Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island) said, adding about the surveillance program, “and that's one of them.”

Some conservatives and libertarian-leaning members routinely argue that communications by Americans get swept up as part of the process, despite provisions in the law limiting who the intelligence community can monitor.

The program was recertified in March by the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court, which allows FISA to continue collecting information under the law for those foreign individuals they already began monitoring. Because the program’s congressional authorization has lapsed, the Trump administration has not been able to open new “orders” under the program.

Intelligence officials have indicated to lawmakers that a FISA reauthorization needs to happen by Thanksgiving in order to avoid a lapse ahead of that March 2027 deadline, a source familiar told The Sun.

“In my view, there's still a sense of urgency,” Thune told reporters earlier in the week.

Despite the tumult that surrounded his nomination, Democrats have indicated that there are winds shifting with Clayton finally in office.

Sen. Mark Warner (D-Virginia), the ranking member on the Intelligence panel, noted that Clayton has been more responsive to committee queries lately, a sign he believes could help move a bipartisan bill.

“Even though I didn’t vote for Jay Clayton, I think the approach he’s taken — he’s communicating better with committees. He’s starting to report some of the things that we’ve been looking for. In my mind, he’s given me more confidence,” Warner told The Sun.

Warner added the current state of play isn’t ideal for the long term so Congress needs to act.

“The challenge that he kind of acknowledges is the fact that the [telecommunications companies] are still cooperating is a very good sign, but there’s no guarantee that will go forever.”

entries.title: Former Falls Church Youth Minister Accused of Sexually Abusing Children
entries.summary: Jeffrey Turner Taylor, 66, faces up to 105 years in prison.
entries.content:
A former youth minister for a Northern Virginia church faces federal child-exploitation charges after he allegedly sexually groomed multiple boys across the country under the guise of spiritual guidance, court documents show.

Jeffrey Turner Taylor, 66, who was arrested in Ohio and made an initial court appearance Monday, previously served as the youth ministry director for The Falls Church from 1990 to 2000 before moving into a family ministry role, which he held until 2002.

The Falls Church, a nearly 300-year-old Episcopal church, was established in 1732 and reconstructed in 1769, with George Washington serving as an early church warden.

During Taylor’s tenure as youth ministry director, he grew the youth program exponentially, which served students in sixth through 12th grade, the arrest affidavit states. The program, named Cornerstone, included weekly small group meetings, large gatherings on Sundays and one-on-one mentorship sessions.

According to court documents, Taylor’s alleged habits of sexually grooming children in his ministry included inquiries into their sexual habits, gift-giving and horseplay. Investigators also allege Taylor traveled with the intent to engage in illicit sexual conduct by taking a boy with him to a ministry event in Chicago.

In 2002, Taylor moved to Atlanta to work at another church, where investigators allege he groomed a boy in his ministry, later sexually abusing him. He stayed in the city until 2013, when he moved to Milford, Ohio. The affidavit alleges Taylor’s grooming and abuse spanned from at least 1990 until 2008.

He is scheduled for arraignment in the Eastern District of Virginia on Sept. 24, and if convicted, faces up to 105 years in prison.

Officials are encouraging anyone with information who may have been a victim of Taylor to contact the FBI Washington Field Office here.

entries.title: House Passes Russia Sanctions Bill After Fight Over Trump’s Tariff Powers
entries.summary: The package targets Russia’s energy and defense industries, financial institutions, senior officials and tankers that had evaded existing restrictions on Russian oil.
entries.content:
The House passed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill Wednesday, giving President Donald Trump new power to punish countries that buy Russian energy.

The House voted 262-159 to approve the Senate-passed legislation without changes. The bill, backed 58 Democrats and all but seven Republicans, now goes to Trump, who is expected to sign it.

The measure, dubbed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, was named for the South Carolina senator, who spent more than a year championing it. His death in July gave the bill new momentum, helping to propel it through the Senate.

The package targets Russia’s energy and defense industries, financial institutions, senior officials and the “shadow fleet” of tankers used to evade existing restrictions on Russian oil.

It also allows Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods from the five largest purchasers of Russian oil or natural gas. China and India are expected to be on that list.

Supporters say the tariffs would force countries to choose between access to the American market and buying Russian energy that helps finance President Vladimir Putin’s war on Ukraine.

“You can evade sanctions, which the Russians have done for years, but you cannot evade tariffs,” Rep. Michael McCaul (R-Texas), who helped shepherd the bill’s passage, said ahead of the vote. “That’s why they are the teeth of this bill.”

The measure also gives Trump broad authority to waive the sanctions, restrictions and tariffs after certifying to Congress that doing so is in the country’s national interests.

Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-New York) opposed the bill alongside other senior Democrats, including Reps. Richard Neal of Massachusetts, the top Democrat on the Ways and Means Committee, and Don Beyer of Virginia, the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee.

They argued the bill would raise consumer prices, give Trump another tool to target U.S. allies and grant him authority he did not need. Trump, they said, already had the power to impose tougher sanctions on Russia but had chosen not to use it.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said ahead of the vote that the legislation “fails to mandate sanctions on Russia.”

“There are so many loopholes written into the bill,” he said, “I believe that it's very unlikely the sanctions relief contemplated in the legislation will ever see the light of day."

Before the bill reached the floor, Democrats pushed several changes.

Meeks sought to remove the bill’s secondary-tariff authority and impose tighter limits on Trump’s power to waive sanctions. He also proposed $15 billion in direct military-financing loans for Ukraine and sought to prevent the administration from treating the European Union as a single country when calculating Russian energy purchases.

With House members preparing to leave Washington until after November’s elections, the Republican-controlled Rules Committee on Tuesday blocked the proposed amendments, keeping the Senate bill intact. Any change would have required another Senate vote and risked delaying final action. The fight then moved to the House floor for a procedural vote, where two Democrats helped rescue the rule after two Republicans defected.

Meeks said the bill would give Ukrainians “false hope.”

“This is going to be a short-term gain for long-term pain for the Ukrainians and the American people,” he said.

The bill is headed to Trump’s desk more than a year after Graham introduced it. It stalled as Trump pursued negotiations with Moscow and Graham worked to secure White House support.

Trump backed a revised version in July, shortly before Graham’s death. The compromise limited tariffs to the largest buyers of Russian energy, preserved presidential waiver authority and extended the Iran Sanctions Act through 2031 at Trump’s request.

The Senate passed it, 86-11, last month. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy lobbied senators and watched an earlier procedural vote from the Senate chamber.

The House had already passed a broader Ukraine package in June. The Ukraine Support Act cleared the chamber, 226-195, but stalled in the Senate. Meeks and other Democrats initially wanted to combine parts of the two bills. Supporters of Graham’s measure warned that doing so could sink legislation that had already won 86 Senate votes and presidential support.

entries.title: McConnell Does Just Enough to Advance Farm Bill
entries.summary: The bill had stalled in committee when the Kentucky Republican was on an extended absence.
entries.content:
Sen. Mitch McConnell missed most of the Senate Agriculture Committee hearing Wednesday, but he entered the meeting at the moment he was needed — to cast the deciding vote that advanced the farm bill.

The Kentucky Republican’s only contribution was an “aye,” as staff and other senators watched closely to make sure he voted so. He then left the room.

In August, McConnell’s absence meant the panel could complete work on the bill since he was voting by proxy, a process that allows another senator essentially to vote on his behalf. Back then, the committee’s Republicans couldn’t send the farm bill to the Senate floor because proxy votes can’t be the deciding vote for a bill to advance.

On Wednesday, the other action at the hearing underscored how the fate of the farm bill remains uncertain, along with the future of its programs and funding that are essential to the agricultural industry.

Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa) tried at the start of the meeting to offer an amendment with language intended to reverse Proposition 12, a California law that requires minimum space requirements for farm animals.

Committee Chair John Boozman said the deadline for introducing amendments had passed at a markup in August. “Everybody understood that we recessed so we could come back and then not have to start over,” Boozman said after the meeting. “All the titles were closed.”

Ernst, along with Sens. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Ray Lujan (D-New Mexico), objected to Boozman not allowing a vote on the amendment.

Sen. John Hoeven (R-North Dakota) suggested amendments could be addressed when the bill is on the Senate floor.

“It’s past time, we’ve got to get to the floor,” Hoeven said.

Senators from both sides of the aisle agreed that it was imperative to pass the farm bill quickly, and each side implored the other to come to an agreement.

“We can’t keep waiting,” Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pennsylvania) said. “America’s farmers are counting on this bill.”

Ranking member Amy Klobuchar said Democrats are remaining firm in their ask for a two-year extension of delaying a cost shift to states for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, arguing that states will be on the hook for hundreds of millions of dollars without a delay.

Majority Leader John Thune and Boozman say their current offer for a one-year delay in the farm bill is better than no delay at all.

“If this doesn’t go anywhere, states will pay 17 billion more,” Thune said. “I don’t understand the resistance from my colleagues on the other side of the aisle.”

The bill needs 60 votes to clear a filibuster — a bar Republicans can’t hit on their own. Boozman said he has heard from some Senate Democrats outside the committee that they would support this version of the farm bill.

Fetterman seemed to signal some potential willingness to take the one-year extension, despite his vote against the bill’s passage. Fetterman said several Pennsylvania farm groups met with his office this week and stressed that the farm bill be passed quickly.

Fetterman didn’t answer questions from reporters after the meeting.

Klobuchar also mentioned cuts to some USDA conservation programs she would like to see reversed, and argued that has support within the Make America Healthy Again movement. Both the House and Senate versions of the farm bill have drawn ire from the MAHA crowd since April.

Congress will need to work quickly to get the bill through before provisions and funding in the current farm bill expire. Farmers are squeezed financially by tariffs, higher input prices — including major cost increases for diesel and fertilizer prices — and extreme weather and drought.

“If the window is going to close — that we are able to get this accomplished — then farmers don’t get help, and you don’t get any help to the states,” Boozman said.

entries.title: Park Service Quietly Awards Contracts for Trump's East Potomac Golf Course Takeover Plans
entries.summary: Rep. Jared Huffman said NPS had hired a civil engineering firm to begin work without public announcement or a heads-up to Congress.
entries.content:
By Matthew Daly

The Trump administration has awarded contracts to begin work on President Donald Trump’s planned takeover of the East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, Democrats on the House Natural Resources Committee said Wednesday.

Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the panel's top Democrat, revealed during a committee hearing that the National Park Service hired a civil engineering firm to begin work on the historic public golf course, without any public announcement or heads-up to Congress. A lawsuit challenging Trump’s plan to revamp the golf course argues that the administration’s redevelopment would violate the congressional act that created the park more than a century ago.

“Now, this is not just any old golf course. This is a beloved public space with huge historic significance," Huffman said.

Trump is “systematically moving to take this historic, publicly accessible resource and turn it into another gilded private golf club for the mega-rich," Huffman said, calling the project “a methodical, deliberate effort to take a public park away from the people," with American taxpayers footing the bill.

A contract approved last week authorizes nearly $400,000 for a Massachusetts-based company to perform environmental and historic preservation compliance work at the course, Huffman said. The park service has since posted a projected construction contract worth up to $49 million, with an expected solicitation date of Jan. 31, 2027.

“Democrats on this committee are tracking all of this. We’re going to keep dragging it all into the daylight until the public gets the answers we deserve," Huffman said in a statement. "We’re not going to let Donald Trump walk off with our public lands. That park belongs to the American people, and I’m not willing to sit here and watch him simply steal it.”

The $389,355 award to Vanasse Hangen Brustlin, Inc., which also has an office in Washington, D.C. and other parts of the country, follows months of activity at the park. The administration has reached an agreement with Fazio Design and undisclosed private and public partners to begin major construction, Democrats said, citing published reports. Trump has said he wants to turn the golf course into a world-class golf venue. It’s part of his grand vision for Washington, D.C., where he has torn down storied structures, remade or renamed others and deployed the National Guard for more than a year.

Huffman, Maryland Reps. Jamie Raskin and Glenn Ivey, along with District of Columbia Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton and Virginia Rep. Don Beyer, sent a letter to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and acting park service director Jessica Bowron demanding all documents, communications and records on the project.

“East Potomac Park does not belong to Donald Trump,” the lawmakers wrote. “It belongs to the American people, and it has for more than a century.”

Spokespeople for the Interior Department and National Park Service did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

entries.title: Troops Must Prepare to Fight Around the Moon, Top Military Adviser Says
entries.summary: Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said the U.S. military should adapt now so it “is prepared to fight, endure and win ... from the seabed to cislunar space.”
entries.content:
By Konstantin Toropin

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. (AP) — American troops need to prepare for combat not only in Earth's orbit but around the moon, President Donald Trump’s top military adviser said Wednesday, looking ahead to a new frontier in warfare after the U.S. revealed for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space.

Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, told service members and industry figures at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference outside Washington that the U.S. military should adapt now so it “is prepared to fight, endure and win ... from the seabed to cislunar space.”

Space Force, the newest military service, which was created by Trump in 2019, is preparing to fight in space and around the moon because “humanity is advancing deeper into space — the Space Force’s job is to help be prepared to defend U.S. interests,” Lt. Gen. Gregory Gagnon, head of the force’s Combat Forces Command, told reporters separately.

The announcement that the U.S. military is ready to fight in the area between high Earth orbit and the moon itself comes days after Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed at the same conference that the U.S. has fielded “on-orbit space control weapons."

The spate of announcements about space weaponry from military officials over recent days flies in the face of long-standing conventions and international understandings that have held outer space as only to be used for peaceful purposes and remain non-militarized.

While multiple nations, including the U.S., have demonstrated the ability to shoot down satellites in Earth orbit, those demonstrations have taken place from the ground against their own satellites.

However, according to Gagnon, “the intelligence community has been clear that potential adversaries have been seeking to extend warfare into space” and that the U.S. military needs to react.

“Our potential adversaries such as the PRC are actively pursuing activities in the system, in parts of space,” Gagnon said, referring to the People's Republic of China, the country's official name.

China established its own military space troops in 2024, charging them with boosting capability to manage space crises.

When asked about the U.S. announcement on deploying weapons in space, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters Tuesday that “China always upholds the peaceful use of outer space, maintains outer space security and opposes the weaponization, militarization and an arms race in outer space.”

Guo also urged the U.S. to “stop expanding its military preparations in outer space.”

It is not clear whether deploying weapons in space or possible plans to use them around the moon will run afoul of international treaties that prevent the militarization of space.

The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, which the U.S. and China have signed, says celestial objects such as the moon are to be used “exclusively for peaceful purposes,” nuclear weapons cannot be placed in space and countries are “liable for damage caused by their space objects.”

There was a renewed push two years ago to further bolster anti-militarization measures in the United Nations following U.S. reports that Russia was developing a space-based weapon.

Russia vetoed a joint U.S.-Japanese resolution that would have called on all countries not to develop or deploy nuclear arms or other weapons of mass destruction in space, as banned under the treaty. A rival Russian resolution to ban all weapons in space “for all time” also ultimately failed.

When asked about the 1967 treaty and other similar obligations, Gagnon said the U.S. Space Force “will continue to execute safe and responsible space operations in all the reaches of space.”

However, he would not say what Space Force or overall U.S. military policy was on the use of weapons like bullets or projectiles in space. He directed questions to the Pentagon, which did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment.

Gagnon also says the U.S. aims to double the size of the Space Force over the next five years — to roughly 25,000 service members — and that about two-thirds of that growth would be focused on Combat Forces Command.

“We have capabilities in the military because we are preparing to defend the nation," Gagnon said. "The reason we have the capabilities is to help create deterrence.”

entries.title: Kamala Harris Will Campaign with Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan
entries.summary: The event marks the pair’s first public appearance together since Harris endorsed El-Sayed after his primary victory.
entries.content:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris will campaign with Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan next week as part of a midterms circuit tour to help Democrats win competitive seats in Congress.

Harris, who endorsed the progressive Democrat following his tight primary win last month, will join El-Sayed for a campaign roundtable about the disparities Black mothers face during and after pregnancy. Recent polling shows El-Sayed faces a tight race against Republican opponent Mike Rogers as Democrats aim to pick off four Senate seats nationwide to win a majority in the chamber.

“Vice President Harris looks forward to returning to Michigan to help turn out the vote in this critical state,” Eduardo Negrón, Harris’ spokesperson, said in a statement. “It is critical we flip the Senate so we can bring down prices and stand up to Donald Trump’s corruption.”

El-Sayed is up against heavy outside spending, and has been a frequent political target for Republicans hoping to maintain control of Congress past November. Vice President JD Vance recently called him “evil,” while Rogers and other Republicans have accused El-Sayed of being an “extremist” backed by terrorist groups.

Harris’ Michigan stop is part of a nationwide tour that includes campaigning with Democrats in her home state of California and Georgia, and marks the pair’s first public appearance together since the former vice president endorsed him.

“Abdul is thrilled to welcome Vice President Harris to Michigan for a conversation about improving Black maternal health and bringing down health care costs,” Roxie Richner, a spokesperson for El-Sayed, told The Washington Sun.

“There’s no better choice for Michiganders than Abdul when it comes to making health care more affordable,” she added. “He’s grateful Vice President Harris will join him in spreading that message.”

entries.title: Judge Scolds ICE Over Investigation of a New York Man’s Critical Email
entries.summary: Federal agents visited the man’s home and tracked him to a hotel after he likened the acting ICE director to a Nazi.
entries.content:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement likely violated a New York man’s freedom of speech when it threatened to criminally prosecute him after he sent a scathing email to the agency’s former top leader, a federal judge in Washington ruled.

U.S. District Judge Rudolph Contreras this week ordered ICE not to act on the “warning notice” that federal agents hand delivered to David Streever that said he “may be in violation of federal law,” according to court documents. The ICE Office of Professional Responsibility, the notice stated, had “reason to believe” that a biting email Streever sent to the then-acting ICE director, Todd Lyons, may have unlawfully threatened a federal official.

If he did not “discontinue” his behavior, the office warned Streever he could face federal and state prosecution, the records said.

Streever sent the outraged email to Lyons following the fatal shooting of 37-year-old Alex Pretti in Minneapolis by federal immigration authorities. Pretti’s killing, which came weeks after agents also fatally shot Renee Good in Minneapolis, further escalated debates about government dissenters’ free speech rights amid tense clashes with ICE agents.

“Americans have long voiced their displeasure with their government,” Contreras said in his ruling. “The Declaration of Independence itself is a list of grievances between Americans and the British government. And Americans have not always indulged in the elevated prose of the Declaration.”

In Streever’s email sent Jan. 26, he called Lyons a “monstrous human being” and compared him to Reinhard Heydrich, a Nazi official who played a key role in orchestrating the Holocaust. Streever told Lyons that the way he was “protecting the obvious execution in Minnesota, even as we see the videos, will lead to your downfall.”

“Even Trump will turn on you before the end, and you will be a sad, despised man who eats himself alive with shame at your own pathetic weakness,” Streever wrote, according to court documents. “You will never know peace. You will seek to lose yourself, to escape the burden of knowing the truth about yourself. But wherever you go, you will find yourself. You will torment yourself until your last day on Earth.”

Federal agents appeared at his house in Rochester, New York, five months later to deliver the warning notice to Streever, but he was returning from a trip to Europe, the records said. Unable to find Streever at his home address, federal agents later appeared at the front desk of a New York City hotel that Streever and his daughter were staying in.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security denied that it has attempted to “squash” free speech.

“ICE investigates all credible threats towards its employees and officers, including threats to the ICE Director,” the spokesperson said in a statement Wednesday.

The Wall Street Journal reported in August that ICE has used a surveillance program to monitor threats towards its agents — a tactic that free speech advocates have decried.

Streever celebrated Tuesday’s ruling in a statement provided by the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, which represented him in court.

“I’m deeply relieved that the court affirmed what I knew all along: that I am permitted to speak my conscience in the United States of America, including when I criticize government officials,” Streever said. “While I wish this ordeal hadn’t happened, hopefully this incident will serve as a reminder that the First Amendment protects us all.”
